chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Black-Scholes Formula, Step by Step

lessons.title: Risk-Neutral Valuation: The Core Idea Behind the Formula

children.text: A Trick That Works Even When Replication Gets Complicated

Lesson 1.3 priced a Reliance call by building a replicating portfolio of shares and borrowed money, by hand, for a single two-outcome step. That works, but imagine doing it separately at every node of the 50-step tree from Lesson 1.4, or in the fully continuous world of Lesson 2.2. Black, Scholes, and Merton needed a shortcut, and the shortcut they landed on, risk-neutral valuation, gives the exact same answer as replication with far less bookkeeping. It is the actual technique behind the formula Chapter 3 is building toward.
The Risk-Neutral World: A Useful Fiction

Imagine a parallel, purely hypothetical market where every investor is indifferent to risk: nobody demands any extra return for holding something uncertain. In that imagined world, every asset, including a risky stock, is expected to grow at exactly the risk-free rate, no more and no less. Real investors obviously do not behave this way; Lesson 1.3 spent real time on the fact that investors demand risk premiums, and disagree about how large those premiums should be. The remarkable result is that you do not need real investors to actually think this way for the trick to work. It turns out that pricing an option by (1) computing its expected payoff using this fictional risk-neutral world's probabilities, then (2) discounting that expected payoff at the risk-free rate, always produces exactly the same price as the honest, no-arbitrage replication argument.

body.text: Risk-neutral probabilities are a calculation tool, not a claim about how anyone actually feels about risk. Nobody is asserting that real investors are indifferent to risk. The claim is narrower and stranger: whatever your real-world risk appetite, the no-arbitrage price of a derivative is identical to the one you would compute by momentarily pretending everyone was risk-neutral.

children.text: Closing the Loop on the Reliance Example

body.caption: p is the risk-neutral probability of the up move. It is built purely from the risk-free growth factor and the two possible prices, never from anyone's actual view on where Reliance is headed.

children.text: Recall Lesson 1.3's numbers: Reliance at ₹2,800 today, landing at either ₹3,000 or ₹2,600 in a month, with a 6% annual (0.5% monthly) risk-free rate. Plugging in: (1.005 × 2,800 − 2,600) ÷ (3,000 − 2,600) = (2,814 − 2,600) ÷ 400 = 214 ÷ 400 = 0.535. So the risk-neutral probability of the up move is 53.5%, and of the down move, 46.5%. Notice this only produces a sensible probability between 0 and 1 because 2,600 < 2,814 < 3,000, the risk-free growth sits strictly between the two outcomes. If it did not, the no-arbitrage condition from Chapter 1 would already be broken.
Now take the expected payoff under these risk-neutral probabilities: 0.535 × ₹200 + 0.465 × ₹0 = ₹107.00. Discount that back one month at the same 0.5% risk-free rate: ₹107.00 ÷ 1.005 = ₹106.47.

body.title: Two roads to the identical price

columns.label: Replication (Lesson 1.3)
points: Build a portfolio of 0.5 Reliance shares plus borrowed money
Size the borrowing so the portfolio matches ₹200 up and ₹0 down exactly
Cost today: ₹1,400.00 in shares minus ₹1,293.53 borrowed

columns.label: Risk-neutral valuation (this lesson)
points: Compute p, the risk-neutral probability of the up move: 0.535
Take the expected payoff using p, not the real-world probability

body.label: Two methods, one number
body.context: Replication and risk-neutral valuation are not two competing theories that happen to agree here. They are algebraically the same argument, written two different ways. Risk-neutral valuation just scales to complicated, many-step, or continuous-time problems far more easily.

children.text: Why the Real-World Probability Never Mattered

A sharp question to ask here: 0.535 was never anyone's actual forecast of Reliance rising. Lesson 1.3 never even specified a real-world probability. So what was 0.535 doing all along? It answers a narrower question than "will Reliance go up". The real-world probability, and the risk premium built on top of it, determines what return the stock itself is expected to deliver on average, which is exactly why different investors can reasonably disagree about whether to own Reliance at all. The risk-neutral probability answers a completely different question: given today's stock price, the two possible future prices, and the risk-free rate, what option price keeps the whole system arbitrage-free? That question has one, unique, non-negotiable answer, regardless of anyone's opinion about direction, because it is really a question about consistent pricing between the stock, the bond, and the option, not a question about forecasting.

body.title: Does a bullish view change the option's fair price?
body.question: Two analysts disagree: one assigns Reliance a 70% real-world chance of rising to ₹3,000, the other assigns it 40%. Using risk-neutral valuation, whose view gives the correct no-arbitrage price for the option in this lesson's example?
options: The 70% analyst, since a bullish view should raise the option's value
The 40% analyst, since a cautious view is more prudent
Neither. The no-arbitrage price uses the risk-neutral probability (0.535 here), not either analyst's real-world forecast
The average of the two, weighted by each analyst's track record
body.explanation: Real-world probabilities describe what each analyst expects the stock to do, which shapes whether they want to own the stock, not what price keeps the option consistent with the stock and the risk-free rate today. That price is pinned by the risk-neutral probability alone, exactly as the replication argument in Lesson 1.3 never needed a probability at all.

body.title: Compute the risk-neutral probability yourself
body.prompt: Same setup: Reliance at ₹2,800, one month, 0.5% monthly risk-free growth. Now suppose it lands at either ₹2,950 (the scenario from Lesson 1.3's delta exercise) or ₹2,700. What is the risk-neutral probability of the up move?
body.explanation: p = (1.005 × 2,800 − 2,700) ÷ (2,950 − 2,700) = (2,814 − 2,700) ÷ 250 = 114 ÷ 250 = 0.456. As a bonus check, discounting the expected payoff (0.456 × ₹150) ÷ 1.005 gives roughly ₹68.06, the same price a full replicating portfolio would produce for this strike.

body.text: Risk-neutral valuation does not claim the world is risk-neutral. It shows that the no-arbitrage price of a derivative can always be written as a discounted expected payoff under one specific, calculable set of probabilities, and those probabilities have nothing to do with anyone's actual forecast.

points: Risk-neutral valuation prices a derivative as the expected payoff under risk-neutral probabilities, discounted at the risk-free rate, and gives exactly the same answer as building a replicating portfolio.
The risk-neutral probability p = [(1+r)S0 − Sd] / (Su − Sd) is built only from observable prices and the risk-free rate, never from a real-world forecast.
In the Reliance example, risk-neutral valuation and replication both land on ₹106.47, confirming they are the same underlying argument, not two independent methods that happen to agree.

Real-world probability determines the return investors expect from holding the stock itself. Risk-neutral probability determines the one price that keeps the stock, the risk-free asset, and the option mutually consistent.
This reframing is what lets the same logic scale from a single two-outcome step, to a multi-step tree, to the fully continuous Black-Scholes formula built later in this chapter.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The Reliance prices, probabilities, and risk-free rate used here are hypothetical, carried over from Lesson 1.3 purely to illustrate risk-neutral valuation, not to represent live market data.
